title: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop
question: Who can turn a model proposal into an environmental action?
scope: The two panels compare who closes the same repair loop; neither grants authority to the model.

steps.title: Manual feedback
steps.description: In panel A, the developer runs commands and carries the terminal error back to the model. The answer alone does not execute a tool.

steps.title: Proposal crosses a boundary
steps.description: In panel B, the foundation model returns a proposal to the agent runtime. The dashed line separates proposing from acting.

steps.title: Dispatch and evidence
steps.description: The runtime grants each action before dispatching it to the sandbox. Tests and linters return evidence to the runtime, which can use it in the next turn.

title: The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map
question: How does one live trajectory differ from learning across tasks?
scope: The approximate computer analogy is an introductory map; model proposals do not inherit processor correctness or execution authority.

steps.title: Proposals and stored state
steps.description: The model and agent memory sit in the live execution band. Context and stored-state exchanges pass through the runtime.

steps.title: The runtime mediates effects
steps.description: Validated calls reach tool use; tools exchange effects and results with the environment. The model does not bypass this path.

steps.title: Across-task changes
steps.description: Evaluated trajectories feed learning, which can return updated weights. Coordinating many trajectories is a distinct across-task activity, rather than another step of one model call.

title: The H·S·A Exposure Space
question: Why do tasks with similar turn counts need different controls?
scope: Positions are illustrative configurations. Closure is the response to exposure, not a fourth coordinate.

steps.title: Read three exposures
steps.description: Horizon counts turns, state describes what persists, and authority describes the consequences of granted actions. A long trajectory is not automatically a high-authority task.

steps.title: Confined repair
steps.description: The repair configuration carries a working copy and workspace authority. Its runtime must isolate those artifacts and enforce the task grant.

steps.title: Durable external effects
steps.description: The remediation configuration has fewer illustrated turns but durable state and irreversible authority. Its consequences demand stronger controls than turn count alone indicates.

steps.title: Read-only still carries risk
steps.description: Support and research are plotted at read-only authority with different horizons and state. Read-only access still requires care about what information can leave the system.

title: Measured Task Horizon
question: What does a measured 50 percent task horizon say about agent reliability?
scope: These are recorded benchmark estimates with confidence intervals. Expert task duration is not an agent’s runtime, and the fitted historical trend is not a forecast.

steps.title: Read the measured quantity
steps.description: The vertical axis gives expert-time task length at which the agent succeeds in half its attempts. It is logarithmic: equal vertical spacing represents multiplicative changes in task length.

steps.title: Distinguish frontier from other evaluations
steps.description: Filled points were frontier models at release; open points were not. Vertical bars retain uncertainty around the measured horizons.

steps.title: Interpret the fitted line cautiously
steps.description: The dashed straight fit on the logarithmic axis represents an exponential historical trend since 2023. It does not show a guarantee of future gains or reliable completion of every task below the horizon.

title: The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle
question: Where can an agent turn wait, execute, or terminate?
scope: This lifecycle is a control-flow map, not a claim that every proposal is authorized or every timeout proves failure.

steps.title: Assemble before calling
steps.description: The runtime assembles context and invokes the model. The resulting proposal proceeds to validation, rather than directly to tool execution.

steps.title: Authorization controls execution
steps.description: Only the authorized path enters tool execution. Approval can pause in Wait; rejection follows the no-execution branch.

steps.title: Evidence drives assessment
steps.description: Tool outcomes feed observation and evidence, then contract assessment. A timeout may leave the outcome unknown, so it is not automatically success or failure.

steps.title: Acceptance is an explicit exit
steps.description: Evidence meeting the contract permits acceptance. Otherwise the runtime may continue another turn, wait, or stop without acceptance.

title: From Agent Context to KV State
question: Why does a longer context reduce the number of resident trajectories?
scope: The displayed token counts and KV quantities belong to the figure’s declared architecture; KV cache is not all accelerator memory.

steps.title: Separate reusable and growing context
steps.description: The shared prefix contains system instructions, tool schemas, and workspace content. Turn history and the active observation extend the serialized context.

steps.title: Retain keys and values
steps.description: Each context token contributes key and value state across the shown heads and layers. The lower arrays depict retained serving state, not a second copy of the prompt text.

steps.title: Scale the footprint
steps.description: The per-token expression includes both K and V; multiplying by context length gives the context’s KV footprint for this architecture.

steps.title: Capacity becomes concurrency
steps.description: The finite pool admits only as many contexts as their footprints permit. Increasing context length reduces this capacity even while the model weights stay fixed.

title: Attention Architecture Sets the KV Payload
question: Why can a larger model retain less KV state per token?
scope: The figure compares declared model geometries at 16-bit precision. Accelerator reference lines show total memory, not memory wholly available to KV state.

steps.title: Compare stored attention state
steps.description: The left panel groups the published geometries by MHA, GQA, and MLA. Parameter count alone does not determine the amount of retained key and value state.

steps.title: Accumulate state over retained tokens
steps.description: Each line in the right panel grows with retained context length for one representative architecture. A lower per-token payload permits a longer context at the same KV capacity.

steps.title: Respect the comparison limits
steps.description: Horizontal lines are whole-accelerator memory references; weights and other runtime allocations also consume that memory. The dotted MHA segment extends beyond that model’s trained window for scale only.

title: Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache
question: Which cached prefix can be evicted without breaking an active request?
scope: The tree distinguishes cached dormant state from a running request’s path; leaf eligibility does not make every dormant ancestor evictable.

active.label: Active shared prefix and repair path

steps.title: Shared ancestors remain useful
steps.description: The active repair path includes the shared prefix and repair history. These ancestors remain live even when other branches are dormant.

steps.title: Choose an eligible leaf
steps.description: Rejected branch and Final turn are dormant leaves in the first panel. Leaf-first eviction avoids removing a prefix that still supports a retained descendant.

steps.title: Return blocks to the pool
steps.description: The second panel removes Final turn while preserving its Other task ancestor. Other task is now a dormant leaf and can become a later candidate.

title: Monolithic vs. Chunked Prefill
question: How can prefill scheduling change the gap between decode tokens?
scope: The two timelines illustrate the shown fixed workload; chunking is not a universal throughput or latency guarantee.

steps.title: One long admission
steps.description: The top panel admits the full 4,096-token prefill as one unit. Ongoing decodes wait across the bracketed gap.

steps.title: Interleave shorter admissions
steps.description: The lower panel partitions the same prefill into eight 512-token chunks. Each iteration also runs the ongoing decodes.

steps.title: Compare gaps, not just completion
steps.description: The triangular markers identify one output token for each ongoing decode. The shorter gaps make the scheduling benefit visible without claiming that prefill work disappeared.

title: Keep, Offload, or Park a Paused Trajectory
question: When should a paused trajectory retain or offload its KV state?
scope: This is the figure’s illustrative decision model with logarithmic axes, not a measured scheduler policy for every machine.

steps.title: Compare wait with transfer
steps.description: The sloped boundary compares expected wait with the KV round-trip transfer time. On the retain side, transferring out and back costs more than the wait.

steps.title: Free device capacity during a long wait
steps.description: Beyond the transfer boundary, the diagram favors offloading to host memory. The worked example locates one context and wait on this side.

steps.title: Host memory is finite too
steps.description: The right-hand boundary introduces host-memory pressure. Very long waits may require parking on flash or dropping state and later recomputing it.

title: The Code Inside the Boundary Is Getting Better at Exploits
question: What does the exploit benchmark trend imply for sandbox design?
scope: The plotted solve rates are benchmark observations under differing agent configurations. Lab-reported points and leaderboard points are distinct evidence sources, not a controlled causal comparison.

steps.title: Read the evidence source
steps.description: Filled points come from the benchmark leaderboard; open points come from model or system cards. The most recent reported gains must be read with that provenance visible.

steps.title: Compare capability across releases
steps.description: Earlier observations cluster lower while later reported configurations solve more tasks without hints. Release date and configuration are observed together, so this is not an isolated intervention on model quality.

steps.title: Contain capable admitted code
steps.description: The dashed step follows the best recorded result to date rather than interpolating every model’s capability. A sandbox must enforce boundaries even when the code it admits is increasingly effective at exploitation.

title: Where Each Boundary Acts
question: Why can a permitted tool still disclose protected information?
scope: The figure contrasts a blocked injected shell request with a permitted reporting channel; passing one control is not whole-system safety.

steps.title: Admission is only the first boundary
steps.description: The injected shell request passes mediation but encounters a filesystem read denial. Different controls act on different capabilities.

steps.title: A blocked path stays blocked
steps.description: The diagnostics destination is not reached along the injected path. The marked upload denial adds a separate egress boundary.

steps.title: Permitted does not mean harmless
steps.description: The submit_report channel is admitted, reads allowed data, and reaches an approved service. Disclosure can still occur through this permitted channel, so policy must consider fields and information flow.

title: Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind
question: What does attenuating one capability change about existing authority?
scope: Derivation narrows a grant; it does not revoke the parent. Caveat verification must check every restriction.

steps.title: Start from the parent grant
steps.description: The edit grant allows read and write on the shown repository prefix until its expiry. This parent remains usable after deriving a child.

steps.title: Reject broader authority
steps.description: The test child attempts execute rights absent from the parent and is rejected. The scan child narrows rights, object scope, and expiry and remains valid.

steps.title: Bind each added caveat
steps.description: The holder appends caveats to the chained authenticator. The verifier recomputes from its key and checks every caveat; possession does not allow deleting an earlier restriction.

title: Where a System Call Lands
question: Where is a workload call mediated under each isolation design?
scope: This comparison locates boundaries, not a universal security ranking or a performance benchmark.

steps.title: A container still reaches the host
steps.description: The shared-kernel container sends calls through a filter to the host kernel. The filter reduces the exposed interface but does not insert a guest kernel.

steps.title: Emulate calls in user space
steps.description: The user-space kernel traps workload calls and emulates them, issuing a reduced set of host calls itself.

steps.title: Separate a guest kernel
steps.description: The microVM runs native calls against its guest kernel. Device I/O crosses the monitor boundary before host interaction.

steps.title: Expose only imported functions
steps.description: Restricted bytecode accesses host functions through runtime imports and linear memory. The permitted imports define the interface that the host must secure.

title: Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest
question: Why does packet filtering need an operation-aware mediator?
scope: The guest has no default route in this design. The pictured approved fetch is a narrow capability, not general repository access.

steps.title: Route to a constrained mediator
steps.description: Fetch approved repo reaches the mediator through the packet filter. The mediator admits the operation and adds the credential outside the guest.

steps.title: Same route, different operation
steps.description: Push or another repo reaches the mediator but is denied there. Address and port controls alone cannot express this operation distinction.

steps.title: Block bypass routes
steps.description: The direct socket is dropped and the name lookup has no resolver route. The metadata host and external DNS server remain unreached.

title: A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse
question: What must finish before a pooled sandbox is safe to lease again?
scope: Ending a trajectory taints its instance; reuse requires the reset contract, not merely process exit.

steps.title: Lease from a trusted baseline
steps.description: A restored instance begins in clean, unassigned standby before one trajectory leases it. End of that trajectory marks it tainted.

steps.title: Remove authority before reset
steps.description: Reclamation fences authority, quiesces owned work, and exports only permitted outputs before discarding or restoring state. This ordering prevents lingering work from writing into a reused instance.

steps.title: Verify or retire
steps.description: Only passing reset-contract checks returns an instance to standby. A failed reclaim step leads to destruction rather than optimistic reuse.

title: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log
question: What can a durable log reconstruct after runtime memory is lost?
scope: Reconstruction folds recorded events only; it does not rerun model or tool calls, and a missing result remains unresolved.

steps.title: Recover from durable events
steps.description: The bottom log retains ordered events after the top runtime memory is lost. TaskStarted through ToolIntent establish what was recorded before the crash boundary.

steps.title: Fold without effects
steps.description: The deterministic reducer applies each event to the initial record. It makes no new model call or tool call during reconstruction.

steps.title: Preserve uncertainty
steps.description: The reconstructed record retains admission and reservation state but marks test_r18 unresolved. A ToolResult beyond the recorded boundary cannot be invented from the intent.

title: Intent Before Dispatch
question: Expose what each crash position permits recovery to conclude about a side effect.
scope: A lost acknowledgment can hide durable intent; after acknowledgment even pre-dispatch crashes are in doubt, and timeout evidence does not settle the outcome.

title: Live Execution vs. Replay
question: How does replay inspect a trajectory without repeating its effects?
scope: Replay follows recorded events and stops on an unlogged request; it is not a fresh sampling run.

steps.title: Live execution produces the record
steps.description: The live harness samples the model and authorizes tools with real effects. Each step appends its corresponding trajectory event.

steps.title: Replay consumes the record
steps.description: The replay harness reads recorded events in order. The model is stubbed and tool execution is disconnected, so replay does not repeat external effects.

steps.title: Stop beyond recorded behavior
steps.description: An unlogged request reaches a stop gate instead of a tool. Missing history remains a boundary of the replay, not permission to improvise a new action.

title: One Model, Many Scaffolds
question: Why does a benchmark score describe an agent configuration rather than just its model?
scope: Rows combine reported configurations on the same benchmark. Their min–max spans are observed scaffold spreads, not confidence intervals or causal estimates of scaffold quality.

steps.title: Hold the model row fixed
steps.description: Each dot on a row is the same model inside a different scaffold. Red diamonds identify the benchmark reference scaffold; the light bar spans the reported minimum and maximum.

steps.title: Inspect a concrete within-model range
steps.description: The annotated Claude Opus 4.6 row runs from 58 to 80 percent. That spread demonstrates why naming only the model omits a consequential part of the evaluated system.

steps.title: Compare configurations with their context
steps.description: Across rows, within-model scaffold spreads can rival differences between models. Report the harness, scaffold, and acceptance procedure alongside the score rather than treating row order as an intrinsic model ranking.

title: Trial Sandbox and Grading Boundary
question: How can an evaluation trial test a candidate without letting it alter the grader?
scope: The sandbox contains the candidate’s trial state; trusted grading criteria and verdict handling remain outside its reach.

steps.title: Isolate each trial’s writes
steps.description: The agent under test edits a copy-on-write layer over a read-only base image. Service fixtures supply controlled interactions; external egress is blocked.

steps.title: Protect acceptance criteria
steps.description: Held-out tests, criteria, and results stay in the trusted controller. The candidate may produce untrusted output but cannot rewrite the grading contract.

steps.title: Bind evidence to the tested workspace
steps.description: The selected workspace ws_r19 reaches candidate execution. Pass, fail, pending, or unknown verdicts remain bound to that workspace rather than to the agent’s own success claim.

title: Neighboring Ranks Are Statistical Ties
question: How much evidence separates neighboring leaderboard ranks?
scope: The figure uses reported standard errors for one evaluator and scaffold. Visual interval overlap alone is not the independent-samples significance test used in the chapter.

steps.title: A point estimate has uncertainty
steps.description: The dot gives tasks resolved and the horizontal bar its 95 percent interval. The top score does not make all nearby configurations distinguishable.

steps.title: Inspect neighboring ranks
steps.description: Neighboring rows have small point differences beside much wider uncertainty intervals. The chapter’s independent-samples comparison, rather than dot ordering alone, assesses whether such differences are resolved.

steps.title: Separate large and small gaps
steps.description: Ranks several places apart can have stronger separation than adjacent entries. These conclusions remain conditional on this evaluator, scaffold, task sample, and reported uncertainty.

title: How Many Tasks an Interval Needs
question: Why can a small evaluation produce a misleadingly narrow interval?
scope: Panel A is a normal-approximation sample-size model for independent tasks; panel B compares interval methods at fixed N = 50.

steps.title: Precision costs independent tasks
steps.description: The left plot shows half-width shrinking as 1 over square root of N. The marked target makes clear that a small improvement in precision can demand many more tasks.

steps.title: Zero observed is not zero uncertainty
steps.description: For 0 of 50 accepted, the Wald interval collapses to zero width. Wilson retains a positive upper bound, acknowledging finite evidence.

steps.title: Inspect behavior near a boundary
steps.description: At 2 of 50, Wald extends below zero while Wilson remains within the probability range. At 25 of 50 the two intervals are much closer.

title: Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns
question: What does each feedback scheme actually establish about an earlier turn?
scope: The fork outcomes are hypothetical sampling evidence. Their difference is not a causal proof; learned step scores change the optimized criterion.

steps.title: One terminal failure cannot separate turns
steps.description: The debugger action and faulty edit lead to the same failed terminal check. With only that check, each shown reward-to-go chip receives the same outcome.

steps.title: Intermediate scores add a criterion
steps.description: The learned scorer supplies per-step scores, but those scores are an added objective. A policy can satisfy the scorer without making task progress.

steps.title: Sample continuations from each fork
steps.description: The bottom panel restores two fork conditions and samples 20 continuations each. One passes from h0 and twelve pass from h1.

steps.title: Keep estimation uncertainty visible
steps.description: The displayed means differ by 0.55, with sampling error. This estimates a difference under the stated continuation procedure and does not establish that the debugger caused success.

title: Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission
question: What is exchanged for higher utilization when rollout slots release asynchronously?
scope: The durations and version bound are illustrative. Version lag bounds do not bound parameter drift or replace objective-specific cohort requirements.

steps.title: Reserved capacity waits at a barrier
steps.description: The short synchronous rollouts finish early but keep slots reserved until the longest member completes. Hatched regions show idle reserved time.

steps.title: Early release creates version lag
steps.description: Asynchronous collection releases slots while the trainer advances versions. A and B remain within the pictured lag bound; C crosses four version boundaries and is excluded.

steps.title: Verification and grouping still matter
steps.description: A rollout receives pass, fail, or unavailable status before waiting in a bounded group buffer. Slot release does not resolve an unavailable verdict or complete a required cohort.

steps.title: Admit with an explicit freshness check
steps.description: The trainer receives a record only through the version-lag decision. Exclusion records reason and cost; a bounded lag still permits distribution drift after large updates.

title: Four Coordination Arrangements
question: Which boundary carries coordination in each arrangement?
scope: Delivery counts describe the declared round patterns; they are not token cost, latency, or mandatory traffic on every actor link.

steps.title: Envelopes and receipts
steps.description: The supervisor sends one envelope down and receives one receipt back per worker. That declared round has 2N deliveries and requires result checking at the supervisor boundary.

steps.title: Bound the queue
steps.description: Pipeline artifacts pass through explicit queue slots between stages. Capacity and downstream progress determine whether an upstream stage can continue.

steps.title: Coordinate shared publication
steps.description: Workers claim tasks and publish versioned artifacts through a shared store. Concurrent claims and publications need explicit state consistency rules.

steps.title: Address messages to mailboxes
steps.description: Actors exchange addressed messages through their mailboxes. The faint full mesh shows possible connections, while solid arrows show only selected messages.

title: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree
question: How should restart scope follow worker dependencies?
scope: Restarts are fresh admitted attempts. They do not erase external effects or bypass cancellation cleanup.

steps.title: Independent siblings continue
steps.description: In the one-for-one card, only the failed middle worker lies inside the blast radius. Its restart creates a new attempt with its own reservation.

steps.title: Coupled siblings stop together
steps.description: In the one-for-all card, the caller failure invalidates the coupled interface and test work. Cancellation stops those siblings before the group restarts from recorded inputs.

steps.title: Bound repeated recovery
steps.description: When declared restart intensity is exceeded, local restarting stops and failure escalates to the parent. More retries are not an unbounded recovery policy.

review_notes: Inspected canonical artwork PNG from the fresh HTML build and local chapter context; original artwork retained.

title: Private Workspaces and Guarded Publication
question: Why is a textually clean merge insufficient for publishing concurrent work?
scope: Worktrees isolate Git working state, not security authority. Publication must validate exact dependencies and the captured integration head.

steps.title: Separate working state and authority
steps.description: Each worktree has files, index, and HEAD while repository storage is shared. The dashed sandbox, not the worktree, scopes worker writes.

steps.title: A clean merge can be semantically stale
steps.description: The caller edits separate files but relies on the base interface. Merging at the changed head preserves that stale dependency unless it is revalidated.

steps.title: Test the exact integration candidate
steps.description: Revalidation precedes building and checking h_candidate. Evidence for an earlier worker tree is not automatically evidence for this combined candidate.

steps.title: Publish against the captured head
steps.description: Atomic update expects h_head and the publication guard. If the head moved, the attempt returns to validation rather than overwriting intervening work.

title: Majority Review Under an Assumed Error Mixture
question: Why can more reviewers leave a substantial false-approval floor?
scope: These curves follow a stipulated beta mixture with fixed marginal error, not a measured law of model ensembles.

majority.label: Three or more approvals among five

steps.title: Hold individual error fixed
steps.description: Both curves start with the same reviewer marginal false-approval rate. Independent errors yield rapidly falling majority error as odd reviewer count grows.

steps.title: Shared difficulty leaves a floor
steps.description: The beta mixture concentrates errors on difficult candidates. Its majority error flattens near the shown probability that latent false-approval propensity exceeds one half.

steps.title: Inspect the count distribution
steps.description: At five reviewers, the mixture increases both the no-approval extreme and the majority-approval region. More reviewers of the same correlated kind cannot substitute for independent task evidence.
